utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody. Please be seated. Let us hear the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Nicholas Koumjian and Ruth Karper for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Branko Lukic, John Ostojic, and Danilo Cirkovic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let me start by saying this: I have the impression there are a number of problems to be resolved as soon as possible. They are all together small issues, but the addition of these small issues may amount to a mountain. And before this is the case, I think it's absolutely necessary to have a meeting how to proceed, taking into account the problems the parties have for the ongoing case. And therefore, I would ask the parties whether it would be possible for them to participate in a 65 ter (i) meeting this afternoon as from 5.00. Let me know after the first break whether this would be appropriate or would disturb your plans for today. What we, no doubt, have to discuss in open court, and I mentioned this yesterday, is the defendant's motion for testimony by videoconference related to five witnesses. May I ask the Prosecution to comment on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we did not oppose the motion based upon the reasons, the cause, given by the Defence. But we share the Court's view that there are disadvantages to our own case, this is disadvantages to cross-examining via videolink. Our preference would be to do the deposition option that was raised if that is possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Related to all the five witnesses. Anything to be added by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. The only request we make is that the Court keep cognizant of the economies that would be warranted by having a deposition taken, and we thought this would be the best avenue proceeding with the videolink as we have with OTP witnesses, and we're taken aback a little bit that the OTP would like to have a different standard applied when it comes to Defence witnesses. We think the cross-examination, if any, would be consistent, as it was with our presentation during their case, through videolink, through live testimony, or through deposition. This Court has insisted on numerous occasions to raise the issue of economies of scale, equality of arms. And when you view this case in hindsight, we ask in its totality that we see that each request made by the OTP was reasonably and justifiably accepted by the Defence. On the other hand, when those same requests were made, there has always been some provisos or exceptions, and not reasonably accepted by the OTP. We believe that the Court will, in determining whether this proceeds by way of videolink or deposition, take into account the exact same factors that they utilise when granting the OTP's request. We still for the totality of the ICTY and this Tribunal that these five witnesses should proceed via videolink testimony and that there's no prejudice whatsoever to the OTP by cross-examining them as we have through the procedure outlined in the Rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: May I just briefly respond: The Defence for the witness that was used videolink during the Prosecution case did not request a deposition. So it's not the case where one was denied for the Defence and granted for the Prosecution. Furthermore, that was a witness, as Your Honours I believe recall, who was basically testifying about being a victim and witnessing crimes. It did not go to issues of the conduct of the accused as these witnesses would. But again, I indicated in the beginning, we do not oppose the motion but our preference is for deposition. We think it will serve all parties better if that is logistically possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just briefly so the record is clear, Witness O who testified by way of videolink could have been and should have been under what counsel himself states perhaps a 92 bis witness. Instead, after the direct examination, the OTP through Ms. Ann Sutherland decided to go far afield from what the parametres of that witness's statements were to try to extract opinion testimony as it relates to our client, Dr. Stakic. The Court allowed an answer. It was favourable to the Defence. Then questioning immediately ceased. The Defence felt since she gave, in our view, favourable testimony that there was no need to cross-examination -- to conduct cross-examination of the witness at that time. We felt at that time, as we did with their 19 92-bis witnesses that the economies should always be viewed and placed on a balanced scale. And therefore, we did not insist that the witness be brought or that we proceed by way of deposition, just so that the record is clear. I think counsel has a right and the Rules provide clearly that the avenues for cross-examination could be and shall be done either through viva voce or through videolink setup. And we think we should proceed in that manner. We are welcome to go and we are happy to go on the field, all of us, and spend a week to ten days there in order to conduct these five depositions if that's the Court's ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The Court will decide on this issue as soon as possible and as soon as practicable. I would appreciate if I could know after the first break if such a 65 ter conference can be conferred this evening at 5.00 because also from this short intervention, it transpires that there are a number of problems that should be resolved immediately. But the place where to do it is, in fact, a 65 ter (i) conference and not open court. May I ask the usher, then, to please escort our witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Pardon me, Your Honour, before the usher does. I think we have another issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it takes time. Continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We did ask to be heard beforehand in connection with the time schedule that the Court has placed on the Defence and the undue burden that it has shifted upon the Defence. Our client has once again informed us that he is not feeling well, that he is under an enormous amount of stress and pressure because of the Court's schedule. With all due respect, we are in the process of preparing a written application to outline clearly and plainly for the Court how the schedule has changed over the last two and a half months from the initial scheduling order to the revised scheduling order, and we would like respectfully to point out to the Court that there is no other case that's currently pending that has the schedule that has been imposed upon us. Similarly, in our written application, we will show for the Court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think you need not to go into details. This is the purpose of why I think it's necessary to confer in the 65 ter meeting, and there it's the place to discuss these issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I can tell the Court now without waiting for a break, we are not available at 5.00. We have to meet with witnesses. And just so that the Court understands and has an appreciation for it, we meet with these witnesses until wee hours of the evening in order to prepare them. We do not have the opportunity, since we don't have any breaks, to meet with them in the field with the counsel and then to have any consultation with our client in connection with that. So it's unfortunate that we will not be able to meet at 5.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What about Thursday at 5.00? You are aware that on Friday, we are not sitting the so-called, emphasise the so-called entire day, because the Defence should be aware that the sitting hours we are practicing now, this has been -- had been the sitting hours during the last eight hours of the existence of this Tribunal. And there's nothing special with this. So taking into account that Friday morning will be available for your necessary discussions with both witness and your client, would be Thursday afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Judge, with all due respect -- with all due respect, I think it's a very, very critical issue that it cannot wait until Thursday. But I also think that the schedule does not permit us. As the Court knows, we do not start at 9.00 perhaps on Friday, but I believe at 10.30 if my recollection serves me correctly. It does not give us the adequate time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's not correct. We are starting on Friday at 14.15.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, my client has insisted that I apply to the Court - and I hesitate to do so with the witness being present here - to make a specific application with respect to his physical condition and his specific concerns. We don't think that it should be delayed, and we should be heard on this issue immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. What you can't say on the one hand side, you are not prepared to participate in the meeting; on the other hand, tell me Thursday would be too late.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'd like to be heard on the issue today, now. I'd like to be heard on the issue now. I asked the Court representatives that we have specifically three issues to raise with the Court. As the practice has been in the last seven, eight years, that's the procedure. I've asked for that. And I was under the apparently misimpression that the Court was advised that we have those issues to raise. We do not have a recourse other than through --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And the clear ruling was that this has to be done in the framework of a 65 ter (i) conference, and not in open Court. And I will ask you to give me as soon as possible a possible date for a 65 ter (i) meeting. I'm available whenever you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm available right now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No. We have to hear the witness. And as you know, to hear witnesses has always priority because of the time they spent in The Hague and offering their free time in order to bring us closer to the truth. And therefore, I don't want to waste any more time at this point in time on this question. I know it's important for you. It's important first of all for Dr. Stakic himself. But we can't use the limited time available in this courtroom for these purposes. Therefore, the Rules provide another possibility, and we have to take this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may just for the record, Your Honour, with all due respect to the witness, this witness or any witness in all due respect does not supersede my client's rights under the Rules of Detention or the Rules prescribed by the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If you once again would have listened carefully and would review the transcript, then you would come to the same conclusion without these unnecessary comments, to put it this way, Mr. Ostojic. May we now proceed. Mr. Lukic, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Marjanovic.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Have you had a good rest?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: May we continue reading?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would like the usher to deliver to the witness four of our documents marked with the 65 ter numbers 262 through 265, please. Can you please place on the ELMO the Document Number 262, please. And give the witness the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Marjanovic, we haven't had time to go through these documents. I know that in the period in question, you were not the managing director in the Ljubija iron ore mine. But I think that when you see the document, you will understand what it's about. Would you please read out the title of the document, tell us who signed the document, and tell us whether you know that this kind of water supply system existed on your premises in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can comment on this document in view of the fact that I was the leader of the project of the construction of the Omarska mine from 1974 to 1979. When the facilities were being built, one of the issues was how to ensure potable water supplies, especially in the canteen, but also in the rest of the plant. The area is an iron ore mine, and for this reason, the wells on the farms, when we checked the water, had a high content of Fe2O3, also MnO, manganese oxide, and all of this is detrimental to health. An analysis was made of the water, and a system was made to design the well large enough to meet the needs of the employees in the mine. I must point out that in one shift, when the mine was being exploited, there were over 350 employees working at any one time. Later on, this was constructed -- the plant was constructed, and we had to have devices to remove manganese and also Fe2O3. There was a strict quality control of the water, and for this reason, this document was drawn up in March 1979. And the title of the document is "operating instructions for the potable water plant of the Omarska mine." The document discusses technical exploitation --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Would you please read the date once again when this project was drawn up.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: March 1987.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The operating instructions refer to several areas, one is the pump enabling the water to circulate through the pipes. Then there are instructions about the electrical power for these pumps, and also a part dealing with the chemical substances used to remove iron and manganese. Control over the plant was performed by the safety and health protection service which employed engineers of various kinds, a hydrogeologist and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. other kinds of engineers. Sometimes it happened that due to negligence, a large amount of harmful substances turned up in the water, and then a technical intervention had to be made. The people who controlled the water drew up records which were delivered to the managing director or the technical director of Omarska who then had to take appropriate measures. When the Omarska mine was to start up, the institutions of the ministry in charge of energy and mining in Bosnia and Herzegovina sent certain commissions which comprised a sufficient number of experts to approve the use of a certain plant, or they would have comments. They would make remarks, and then the deficiencies would have to be removed before the plant could be started up. At the end of the document, it says: "Omarska, March 1987, instructions approved by the service for protection at work, engineer Franjo Galunic, and also technical director of Omarska, Zdenko Ceraj, graduate mining engineer."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us the ethnic background of these two people?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. They are both Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The next available number would be D66. Correct? Then this document is provisionally marked D66A and B respectively.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could the usher be so kind and show the witness the next document marked with our 65 ter number 263, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marjanovic, can you explain this document briefly, as you have explained the previous one.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can explain it. But I have to mention that I made a mistake just a moment ago because I mentioned the republican ministry for energy and mining. At the time, it was called the republican committee for energy and mining. That was the mistake I made. I mentioned that a commission was set up by the committee for energy and mining of the socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the document contains the number and the date of issue, and the decision refers -- or rather, the decision is to the effect that the well and the potable water supply system can be put into operation. The signature is the assistant president of the republican committee for energy and industry. At the time, this was Dr. Safet Cicic, an acquaintance of mine. If you want to know his ethnic background, I think you do, he is a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This would be D67A, B respectively.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The next document would be the document marked with our 65 ter number 264.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marjanovic, this document is short. Would you please read it and explain it to us, please.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "DP, RJR, Ljubija/Prijedor." DP means socially owned enterprise. "Workplace safety service, Prijedor. The 122nd of November, 1990. 156/90." Minutes: "On the 7th of November, 1990, water samples for bacteriological analysis were taken. The water is bacteriologically satisfactory and correspond to the regulations on potable water quality. "On that occasion, the 7th of November, 1990, I visited the source of the local waterworks of the economic unit of the Omarska mine and found the following situation: "Neither prechlorination nor final chlorination are functioning. Iron and manganese elimination from potable water are not being performed. There is no disinfecting of water because there is no chlorination. Of all the installed water treatment equipment, only the sand filters are functioning. The water disinfection equipment must be made operational as we can never know -- as we can never know when secondary water pollution may occur with all the accompanying health and legal problems." And as miners says, it says "Good Luck. Workplace safety service, Faruk Cerimagic, graduate engineer of technology." And his signature follows. The ethnic affiliation of Mr. Cerimagic, an acquaintance of mine, is a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether Mr. Cerimagic's demands were met?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can assume that this was mandatory. That this had to be complied with because there were rigorous sanctions involved in the mine. A large number of people used this water, so I am sure that there must have been an intervention following this. But I can't guarantee this because I have no personal knowledge of it. I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This document would be marked provisionally as D68A and B correspondingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There is one document left referring to this area. And the 65 ter number is 265. We don't have a translation for this document. We received it, along with the others, from the OTP. Mr. Marjanovic, it will be a bit harder to read out this document because the end is not legible. But I ask you to try and tell us what its contents are.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. "The iron ore -- the Ljubija/Prijedor mine, the service for protection at work, number 86/90, Prijedor, 15th of June, 1990. "Omarska mine economic unit. "Omarska. To the attention of Branko Micic, graduate mining engineer. "Please find enclosed bacteriological water from your water supply system. The analyses are negative, and the findings, I assume that it's probably in accordance with the regulations for potable water, Official Gazette of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia 33/87. I assume that's what it is. The analyses are made at the source in the wet area and in the canteen once a month. Good luck. "Technologist, Faruk Cerimagic, graduate engineer and head of the service for protection at work. Smail Zahirovic, graduate engineer of mining." Both are these are Muslims. And it says: "Deliver one copy to the addressee and one copy to the archives."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This document would be provisionally marked D69B. And it should be mentioned that a provisional translation can be found on the 12th and 13th page of today's transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me just ask you, is it evident from this document that on the 15th of June, 1990, although part of the document is missing, that it can be concluded that the water was potable?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, assuming that they complied with what was previously found about the deficiencies in the water supply system for the Omarska mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would like to cover a different area now and ask you if you know the following: As you took part in the work of the bodies of municipal administration, do you know respectively the positions of the president of the Municipal Assembly, what are the president of the Municipal Assembly's tasks?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sorry. I object. It's vague as to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please answer what the tasks of the president of the Municipal Assembly are and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May you please wait until the Trial Chamber has decided. I'm surprised what's happening on this side of the Defence during the last days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Following deliberations, objection sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll restate the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marjanovic, do you know what the tasks and functions were of the president of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor in the period of time of 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never myself the president of the Municipal Assembly obviously, but the statute of the Municipal Assembly contains clear regulations governing his work in quite a specific manner. So as I had to be familiar with the statute, I think I am to a certain extent qualified to comment on the duties and tasks of the president. I would even go as far as to say that the competencies and authorities from the 1980s, that the president had in the 1980s, and those that he had in the 1990s are almost the same, almost identical. I think the same statute was kept to the end, to the very end of the war. I think it may have been changed but only recently, only very recently. I think what needs to be pointed out is that the president of the Municipal Assembly is elected at a session of the assembly. Usually, it has to be a prominent citizen highly regarded, both as a man and as a humanitarian person. A person, a citizen with certain merits. According to the statute, the president presides over the assembly -- over the sessions of the Municipal Assembly when these sessions are held. He sets the date for the sessions of the assembly, and he convenes the sessions; however, the agenda discussed at the assembly is drafted and proposed by the Executive Board, the Executive Board representing executive authority. The Executive Board demands from the president of the Municipal Assembly that the Municipal Assembly or the Municipality discuss a number of issues, usually such issues as taxes, revenues, and so on and so forth. During the assembly's work, or before the work of the assembly begins, the agenda is debated. And the deputies choose to either adopt or reject certain items placed on the agenda following which the items of the accepted agenda are debated during the session by deputies. Documents are drafted following the debates, the assembly debates, and the documents that result from that are decisions of the Municipal Assembly which are then forwarded to the Executive Board for implementation. The task of the president of the Municipal Assembly is to mediate and to work with the technical services of the Municipal Assembly which, if my memory serves me well, is managed and controlled by the secretary of the municipality. I think this more or less comprises the essential tasks of the president of the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During the time the Crisis Staff existed, did you ever have the impression that the Executive Board was functioning, operating, at the same time? And can you please explain where the secretaries of the secretariat were sitting, in their own offices or perhaps in a different place?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question about the operation of the Executive Board, whether it was working, I can't give you an answer because I don't know if they had any meetings. But all the secretaries, that is, most of the secretaries that I used to see stayed in their offices and performed their duties, the duties of their respective secretariats. I myself went to see the secretary for the economy. I think it was Ranko Travar. In a manner of speaking, he was my superior minister in the municipality. So that was the reason why we had contacts throughout that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us please return to the department of your own enterprise in Omarska, at the time when an investigation centre was operating there. In that period of time, who was in charge of supplying goods, fuel, for example, to that particular section of the enterprise? Was it done through your own offices, if you could please explain that? What did you have up there? Who was using the services of the petrol station?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly how this was happening, because that was completely cut off at that time. But I know that there was a certain amount left behind in the storage rooms of the petrol station. Petrol stations were own by the Energopetrol company, a state-owned company, distributing petrol and oil derivatives. I may be wrong, but I think the quantities we are talking about are quite considerable, I think about 30 tonnes. In earlier times, the petrol station was run by people from the iron ore mine in Omarska. There were people there who issued petrol with clear instructions to document, register, the exact number of vehicles issued petrol, the name of the driver. And it was mandatory to take the driver's signature and the specified quantity of petrol taken. Throughout the period when the investigation centre was operating, I have no information concerning that, nor was I ever informed by anyone. I'm not sure if it was the people who were working there informing the managing director of the Omarska iron ore mine, Dusko Vlacina. I'm not sure they did inform him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the trucks that were owned by your company in Omarska were being used for?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must try to draw a distinction here for my own benefit. The Ljubija iron ore mine owns a considerable number of different vehicles, small trucks with different capacities between 1 or 2 tonnes, and 70 tonnes. The range is as wide as that. However, speaking of Omarska, the enterprise owns a wide range of different vehicles. I will try to enumerate them for you so you know what they are used for. The Caterpillar, the dumpers with 75-tonne capacity for transporting the ore. We had a vehicle for transporting explosives, the capacity 4 and a half tonnes. It was exclusively used for taking the explosives used during mining from Ljubija to the mine, to the pit itself. There were maintenance vehicles there, reparation and maintenance. TAM vehicles, that was the make of the vehicle. We used to refer to them as TAMici. They were between 1.500 and 2.000 kilograms capacity. They had what we used to call Trambus Kabina. It was sort of a long cab which apart from the driver seats perhaps four, five, or up to even six people. The body of the vehicle itself, certain spare parts could be attached to it, and diggers could be towed by this type of vehicle. That's what these special vehicles and machines are used for. They are used as tow vehicles for towing or tugging both the goods and transporting the people who worked there. Excuse me, if I may just add something: There were three different production mines. The eastern mine, the southern mine, and Omarska itself. Those were more or less the same production mines with more or less the same equipment. Maybe the number of equipment differed from one to the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For the sake of the transcript, in order to clarify, did you say southern mines or central mines?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I say southern, I may have made a mistake. Central mines Ljubija. We call them central because all the other production mines developed from that central, original one, the main production mine. So central, eastern, and Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So in the summer of 1992, did you know what the trucks at the mine were being used for? Did anyone inform you about that?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No one provided any kind of information to me. I don't know what those trucks were being used for. I can only assume. The whole production line in the depth of the Omarska excavation mine had to be kept in operation constantly as at that time, there was not sufficient electricity. I suppose maintenance workers there had to -- had to redirect a certain amount of electricity to the generator supplying electricity for the mine. So I suppose they were using some of the vehicles to go to the pit, to the excavation mine and perform those tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you, or actually your company, around Tomasica and Omarska, were you ever robbed around spring, summer, or autumn of 1992?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I will try to tell you exactly what happened. Please try to understand that perhaps I'm not able to provide very precise time coordinates. But I know that the 6th Sana Brigade, in the course of their military operations, reached the central mine, and they wreaked havoc there, useless havoc. They took away all the glue supplies, which is of no use to anyone outside the iron ore mine itself. They took some of our tools and equipment, which are completely useless for any tasks outside the mine. They fired shots at water tanks and at the electricity station. I suppose they were taking away oil from there. They took whatever they could lay their hands on. I don't think that they meant to use these things for the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. work of their unit. I think it was pure hubris. The same unit was staying in the area of the eastern mines towards the end of the war where again they caused an enormous amount of damage. They destroyed the lab, the laboratory which performed analysis of the iron ore quality, the iron ore we were producing. In Omarska, several robberies of private character took place, of private nature. It did happen on certain occasions that armed groups consisting of two or three people would force guards, security guards, to lie down. They would then take keys from them, and they would then go into storage rooms and simply loot the storage rooms, take away things and goods from the storage rooms. They took 12 sets of "zol" keys. Each of them is worth $4.000. They stripped the electricity poles of the 220 volt electricity system part of the structure, which caused two of the poles to collapse. They used this equipment to make baskets, containers, for their tractors. At a later stage, in 1996, I issued an announcement to the citizens of Omarska saying that whoever brings back the sets of stolen keys would be amply rewarded and explaining that the keys were otherwise useless to them. I had no one to complain to about the behaviour and actions of the 6th Sana Brigade. There was no one to complain to, nor would I have been given any attention if I had. I did send written reports to the public security centre of the MUP in Prijedor, but they took no measures whatsoever in this specific case. In order to explain the whole context, the overall situation, they were quite eager, they seemed quite eager when they accused me and my colleagues of having sold parts of the equipment off to Serbia. Simo Drljaca sent over two inspectors who went to Ruma, Kolubara, the Neksic iron factory investigating what we had allegedly sold them, it was scrap iron. Four months later, the inspectors came to see me. Their eyes were full of tears. They said: "Ostoja, please, please admit to something because if you don't admit to anything we will be fired if we don't find anything." But they didn't find anything. I think this very amply illustrates the modus operandi of those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you please repeat whose work this illustrates.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The work of Mr. Simo Drljaca who was at the head of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After the police took over the Omarska mine complex, do you know who operated the petrol pump?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. I don't know. And to be quite honest, I didn't know fully even before that. Those were people who worked there. The foreman designated them, and they had the director of Omarska, and then they had the foremen, and they designated the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would also like to ask you about the kitchen, preparing the food which was near the Separacija. Do you know who ran the kitchen at the time?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. Previously, this was done by a canteen service which delivered food at the level of the whole company, and they had cooks who prepared the food. However, in this period, I have no information nor did anybody inform me, nor was I able to know who did this and how they worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You spoke of the guards at the entrance to the buildings. Who organised the guards and who was there with you in front of your building?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the events at the end of May, and the attack on Prijedor on the 30th of May, there was a situation of chaos. One didn't know where danger might be coming from. And people organised themselves on their own initiative and kept watch at their entrances. They even put iron bars on their front doors. I also kept watch. On several occasions, Ivo Komljenovic kept watch with me. We have already mentioned him. He's a Croat. And then there was Minka Cehajic, a lady who was a doctor and who lived in the same entranceway, and she was there with us. The purpose of this guard duty was for us to be able to raise the alarm if anything happened. We would chat and drink coffee throughout the night. And fortunately, at the entrance to our part of the building, nothing ever happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have already mentioned Mr. Ivo Komljenovic. Now you have mentioned him again. Would you please explain to us how he left Prijedor, who helped him, and why he left.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ivo Komljenovic was a neighbour of mine, a mining engineer. He was the technical director of Nemetal. I think we looked at the document yesterday where he signed for the employees, the work force. He had two small children and a wife. We were on visiting terms. In 1992, in June or July and further on, there was no production. The situation did not promise anything good. You couldn't expect any payments of salaries because I have already said, we were not able to collect the payments for everything we had exported to Zenica. He, I think, had two or three brothers in Germany, and his wife also had relatives there. He contacted them, and they sent him documents. I think the documents arrived through Caritas, the charity organisation. When he received the documents, he asked me whether he should go. I couldn't tell him. I said: "If I tell you to go and this turns out not to be a good decision, I will be to blame for this. If I tell you to stay and things don't turn out well, again, I will be the one to blame." I told him he should decide for himself. And he made up his mind. He asked me to help him. I transported him and his family. We used his car and another car as far as Dvorna Uni, and he went to Vojnic, and after that, he went on towards Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does Mr. Komljenovic ever contact you?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He contacted me from Wiesbaden during the war. He now lives in Zagreb. He is back from Germany, and he visited Prijedor a few times from Zagreb. I didn't know that his wife has said a lot of bad things about me, but this is of no interest now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In order to go from Prijedor toward Croatia, did these people have to have passes?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were supposed to have passes. At the time, checkpoints were set up in places where they were needed and also where they were not needed. I am aware now that some of these checkpoints served for looting purposes. I received documents for Ivo and Dragica Komljenovic, and that's how we managed to pass through all the checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just for the record, in the index of seized documents that we received from the Prosecution, in the section PS, II, 45, on page 45, ERN numbers P0050095 and P0050096, there is a trace that Mr. Marjanovic requested and got the passes for those two persons. Now I'd like the usher to show the witness document -- we have to find the number first, sorry. We will move on and be back with this document later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Although this has nothing to do with this topic, I would like to ask you now whether you heard of the existence of one or more interventions platoons in the municipality of Prijedor and in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have heard of the term Intervention Platoon, which is established in units carrying out war operations. Brigades had Intervention Platoons and even battalions, I think. In military terms, an Intervention Platoon is the first to go into battle and is supposed to break through the enemy defences so that advances can be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether there was an Intervention Platoon in the municipality of Prijedor commanded by the Crisis Staff or later on the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know. I think no such platoon existed, and I would have heard about it because I lived there. But I never heard of any such platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It has not entered the record, so I will repeat my question. Did you say that if such a platoon existed, I would certainly have heard about it?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of what I have said before, anything that happened in Prijedor at the time and that I heard about, I commented on. In view of my role as managing director of the mine, I'm sure, a hundred per cent sure, I never heard about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now we can turn to the -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not accusing counsel of any ill intent. But it counsel speak to each other in their own language loud enough for the witness to hear, there's obviously a potential that it could influence the answers of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I didn't want to interrupt at this point in time. But in fact, we have to speak in the courtroom in a language we understand. It's no doubt the possibility to speak with your client, if necessary, and nobody has any right to listen to this. But to inform maybe -- we don't know what's happening -- the witness on the expected answer by speaking in a language which is not an official language of this Tribunal is a method that should be at least be discussed as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, thank you. And I appreciate that my learned friend warned us. But it can be checked from the audiotapes that the witness has already said what I asked him later on, only it was not reflected in the transcript. So it's very easy to check it that he said the same thing previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just so the record is clear, the interpreter did not translate the witness's specific statements where the witness said that. So for purposes of clarity, we just wanted that suggested. But certainly the interpreters in their booth specifically on page 24, line 8, we invite them to review the audiotape so they can then correct that mistake as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please calm down and take the tone necessary for the courtroom. And this is not a joke, Mr. Ostojic. I asked you to behave as it can be expected from a Defence counsel in this courtroom. And if you have problems with the translation, we had during the last 112 days always a method how to resolve the problem. And this was to ask the booth whether there was a mistake or not. And please stay to the rules and obey the rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may just briefly, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No, not in the moment. The Defence asked for an immediate hearing on procedural issues. Therefore, based on Rule 65 ter (i), I hereby convene a meeting of the parties starting in 5 minutes in my office. The trial stays adjourned until further notice. May I ask the parties and the participants to be prepared to be back in the courtroom at 11.00 sharp, and if there should be any delay I'll let you know. --- Proceedings adjourned at 10.23 a.m. to be reconvened sine die 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
